title: Carbon and Functional Groups
description: Why carbon is special and how functional groups define chemical behavior

concepts.title: Carbon's Unique Bonding
concepts.contentHtml:
Carbon (C) is the backbone of life because it can form four covalent bonds in any direction — creating chains, rings, and branching structures of almost unlimited variety. No other element comes close to this versatility.

Carbon can bond to other carbons repeatedly, producing skeletons from methane (CH₄, one carbon) to polymers with thousands. It also bonds readily to hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur, and halogens. This combinatorial richness is why there are millions of known organic compounds, compared to far fewer inorganic ones.

concepts.title: Functional Groups
concepts.contentHtml:
A functional group is an atom or group of atoms attached to the carbon skeleton that gives the molecule its characteristic reactivity. The carbon chain is mostly inert — the functional group is where the chemistry happens.

Key groups to recognise:
— Hydroxyl –OH: alcohols (ethanol)
— Carbonyl C=O: aldehydes and ketones
— Carboxyl –COOH: carboxylic acids (acetic acid)
— Amino –NH₂: amines and amino acids
— Halide –X (F, Cl, Br, I): alkyl halides

Molecules with the same skeleton but different functional groups have completely different properties and reactions.

concepts.title: Hydrocarbons: Alkanes, Alkenes, Alkynes
concepts.contentHtml:
The simplest organics contain only C and H. Their names follow systematic IUPAC rules based on the chain length and bond type:

Alkanes — all single bonds (saturated): methane, ethane, propane. Formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂. Very unreactive except combustion.
Alkenes — one or more C=C double bonds: ethene (ethylene, CH₂=CH₂). Formula CₙH₂ₙ (with one double bond). Reactive at the double bond via addition reactions.
Alkynes — one C≡C triple bond: ethyne (acetylene, C₂H₂). Very reactive; used in welding torches.

The degree of unsaturation (double/triple bonds, rings) tells you how many hydrogens are 'missing' relative to the saturated formula.

title: Aromatic Chemistry
description: Benzene, delocalisation, and electrophilic aromatic substitution

concepts.title: Benzene and Aromaticity
concepts.contentHtml:
Benzene (C₆H₆) is a hexagonal ring of six carbons, each bonded to one hydrogen. What makes it special is that the six π electrons are delocalised — spread equally around the ring rather than localised in three alternating double bonds. This gives benzene unusual stability called aromaticity.

Hückel's rule: a ring is aromatic if it is planar, fully conjugated, and has 4n + 2 π electrons (n = 0, 1, 2…). Benzene: 6 electrons, n=1. Naphthalene: 10 electrons, n=2. Cyclopentadienyl anion: 6 electrons. Aromatic molecules resist addition reactions and prefer substitution, which preserves the delocalised system.

concepts.title: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution (EAS)
concepts.contentHtml:
Because the benzene ring is electron-rich (delocalised π cloud), it attracts electrophiles. The key mechanism is electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS):

1. The electrophile (E⁺) attacks the ring, forming an arenium ion (carbocation) — the rate-determining step.
2. A proton is lost to restore aromaticity.

Common EAS reactions:
— Nitration: benzene + HNO₃/H₂SO₄ → nitrobenzene (NO₂ substituent)
— Halogenation: benzene + Br₂/FeBr₃ → bromobenzene
— Friedel–Crafts alkylation: benzene + RCl/AlCl₃ → alkylbenzene
— Sulfonation: benzene + SO₃/H₂SO₄ → benzenesulfonic acid

concepts.title: Directing Effects
concepts.contentHtml:
Substituents already on a benzene ring influence where the next group attaches — ortho/para or meta — and whether they activate or deactivate the ring toward further EAS.

Ortho/para directors (activating): groups that donate electrons to the ring (–OH, –NH₂, –OR, –alkyl). They make the ring more reactive and direct incoming electrophiles to ortho and para positions.
Meta directors (deactivating): groups that withdraw electrons (–NO₂, –CN, –COOH, –SO₃H). They make the ring less reactive and direct to the meta position.

Halogens (–Cl, –Br) are unusual: deactivating (electron-withdrawing inductive) but ortho/para directing (electron-donating resonance).

title: Nucleophilic Substitution and Elimination
description: SN1, SN2, E1, E2 — how alkyl halides react

concepts.title: SN2: Bimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution
concepts.contentHtml:
In an SN2 reaction, a nucleophile attacks the carbon bearing the leaving group in a single concerted step — back-side attack — simultaneously displacing the leaving group.

Key features:
— Rate = k[Nu][substrate] (second order)
— Inversion of configuration at the carbon centre (Walden inversion)
— Favoured by: primary substrates, strong nucleophiles, polar aprotic solvents (DMF, DMSO, acetone), good leaving groups (I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻)

Steric hindrance crushes SN2: tertiary substrates react negligibly because the nucleophile cannot reach the electrophilic carbon. SN2 is the mechanism behind many lab syntheses — fast, clean, stereospecific.

concepts.title: SN1: Unimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution
concepts.contentHtml:
In SN1, the leaving group departs first to give a carbocation intermediate, which the nucleophile then attacks in a second step.

Key features:
— Rate = k[substrate] only (first order — nucleophile concentration irrelevant)
— Racemisation (or partial inversion) at chiral centres, since nucleophile attacks both faces of the planar carbocation
— Favoured by: tertiary (and sometimes secondary) substrates (carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1°), polar protic solvents (water, alcohols — stabilise the carbocation), weak nucleophiles

Carbocation stability follows: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl, due to hyperconjugation and inductive donation from alkyl groups.

concepts.title: Elimination: E1 and E2
concepts.contentHtml:
Elimination reactions compete with substitution. Rather than the nucleophile attacking carbon, a base removes a proton on a carbon adjacent to the leaving group, forming a C=C double bond (an alkene).

E2 (bimolecular): concerted, second order, requires anti-periplanar geometry (H and leaving group 180° apart), favoured by strong bulky bases (e.g., t-BuO⁻) and high temperature.
E1 (unimolecular): stepwise, carbocation intermediate, first order, same conditions as SN1.

Deciding between SN2/SN1/E2/E1: primary + strong nucleophile → SN2; primary + strong base + heat → E2; tertiary + weak nucleophile/polar protic → SN1/E1 mixture; tertiary + strong base → E2 dominates.

title: Carbonyl Chemistry
description: Aldehydes, ketones, esters, and nucleophilic addition

concepts.title: The Carbonyl Group
concepts.contentHtml:
The carbonyl group (C=O) is the most important functional group in organic chemistry. Its polarisation — carbon is δ+ because oxygen is more electronegative — makes the carbon a good electrophile and the oxygen a good site for hydrogen-bond acceptance.

Carbonyl compounds by class:
— Aldehyde: –CHO (terminal; e.g., ethanal, benzaldehyde)
— Ketone: internal C=O flanked by two carbons (e.g., acetone, cyclohexanone)
— Carboxylic acid: –COOH (e.g., acetic acid)
— Ester: –COOR (e.g., ethyl acetate)
— Amide: –CONR₂ (e.g., acetamide, peptide bond)

concepts.title: Nucleophilic Addition to Aldehydes and Ketones
concepts.contentHtml:
Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition: a nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbonyl carbon, breaking the π bond and adding across the C=O.

Important reactions:
— Grignard reagents (RMgBr) add to carbonyls → alcohols after workup. A powerful C–C bond-forming reaction.
— Cyanohydrin formation: HCN adds to give –OH and –CN.
— Reduction: NaBH₄ delivers H⁻ to the carbonyl → primary (from aldehyde) or secondary (from ketone) alcohol.
— Acetal formation: two equivalents of alcohol add, expelling water, giving R₂C(OR')₂ — used as a protecting group.

Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones because they are less hindered and have a less electron-donating substituent.

concepts.title: Enols, Enolates, and Aldol Condensation
concepts.contentHtml:
Carbonyl compounds with α-hydrogens (H on the carbon next to C=O) can be deprotonated by base to form an enolate — a resonance-stabilised carbanion. Under acid conditions, tautomerisation gives the enol form.

The aldol reaction exploits enolate nucleophilicity: an enolate attacks the carbonyl of another aldehyde or ketone, forming a β-hydroxy carbonyl compound (aldol product). On heating, the aldol dehydrates to an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl compound (conjugated enone) — the aldol condensation.

Aldol is used industrially (e.g., synthesis of 2-ethylhexanol for plasticisers) and biologically (aldol step in glycolysis uses aldolase enzyme).

title: Stereochemistry and Spectroscopy
description: Chirality, enantiomers, and identifying molecules with NMR

concepts.title: Chirality and Enantiomers
concepts.contentHtml:
A carbon with four different substituents is a stereocentre (chiral centre). The two non-superimposable mirror-image arrangements are enantiomers. Like left and right hands, they are identical in composition but different in three-dimensional shape.

Enantiomers are named using the R/S (Cahn–Ingold–Prelog) system: assign priorities 1–4 to substituents by atomic number; if reading 1→2→3 is clockwise with the lowest priority (4) pointing away, the centre is R (rectus); anticlockwise = S (sinister).

Enantiomers have identical physical properties except one: they rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions. They can have dramatically different biological activities — (R)-thalidomide is a sedative; (S)-thalidomide is teratogenic (though the two interconvert in the body, so neither pure form is safe).

concepts.title: Diastereomers and Meso Compounds
concepts.contentHtml:
Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other. A molecule with two stereocentres can have up to 2² = 4 stereoisomers (2 pairs of enantiomers). Diastereomers have different physical properties (melting point, solubility) and can be separated by ordinary methods.

A meso compound has stereocentres but an internal plane of symmetry — the two halves are mirror images of each other — so the molecule is achiral overall. Meso-tartaric acid is the classic example.

The maximum number of stereoisomers for n stereocentres is 2ⁿ, but meso forms and other symmetry elements reduce this count.

concepts.title: ¹H NMR Spectroscopy
concepts.contentHtml:
Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) is the most powerful tool for determining organic structures. In ¹H NMR, hydrogen nuclei in different chemical environments absorb radiofrequency radiation at different frequencies, reported as chemical shift (δ, ppm relative to TMS).

Key principles:
— Chemical shift: electronegative groups deshield nearby H, shifting peaks downfield (higher δ). Alkyl H ~0–2 ppm; vinyl H ~4.5–6 ppm; aromatic H ~6.5–8 ppm; aldehyde H ~9–10 ppm.
— Integration: peak area ∝ number of equivalent H atoms.
— Splitting (n+1 rule): a proton with n equivalent neighbouring H atoms appears as n+1 lines (doublet, triplet, quartet…).

Together these three parameters uniquely fingerprint most organic molecules.

title: Pericyclic Reactions
description: Concerted bond reorganization through cyclic transition states

concepts.title: What Is a Pericyclic Reaction?
concepts.contentHtml:
A pericyclic reaction proceeds through a cyclic transition state in which all bond changes happen simultaneously — no intermediates, no ions, no radicals.

Three main classes: cycloadditions (Diels-Alder is the prototype), electrocyclizations (a chain closes to a ring), and sigmatropic rearrangements (a sigma bond migrates).

Pericyclic reactions are stereospecific — the geometry of the starting material dictates the geometry of the product, often with high precision.

concepts.title: Woodward-Hoffmann Rules
concepts.contentHtml:
Robert Burns Woodward and Roald Hoffmann (1965) showed that pericyclic reactions are governed by the symmetry of the molecular orbitals involved.

For a [4+2] cycloaddition like Diels-Alder, the rule is 'thermally allowed' (4π + 2π = 6π electrons, suprafacial on both components). [2+2] photochemically allowed but thermally forbidden — so two ethylenes don't fuse on heating, but they do under UV light.

Hoffmann shared the 1981 Nobel for this work; Woodward had died in 1979 (and Nobels can't go posthumously).

concepts.title: Diels-Alder & Click Chemistry
concepts.contentHtml:
The Diels-Alder reaction (Otto Diels and Kurt Alder, 1928 Nobel 1950) joins a diene and a dienophile to give a cyclohexene with up to 4 new stereocenters in one step. 100% atom economy. Indispensable in natural product synthesis.

K. Barry Sharpless's click chemistry (Nobel 2022, his second after 2001) emphasizes reactions that are fast, clean, and reliable — exemplified by the copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC), a [3+2] cycloaddition that's now ubiquitous in chemical biology.

title: Asymmetric Synthesis
description: Making one enantiomer at a time

concepts.title: Why Chirality Matters
concepts.contentHtml:
Many drugs are chiral — they have a 'left-handed' and 'right-handed' form. Often only one is biologically active; the other is inactive or, occasionally, harmful.

The thalidomide tragedy (1950s-60s) — one enantiomer was a sedative; the other caused severe birth defects — drove home the point (even though the two enantiomers interconvert in the body). Modern regulators require chiral drugs to be marketed as single enantiomers when possible.

Synthesis must therefore deliver enantiomerically pure products. Resolution (separating racemates) is wasteful — you throw away half the material. Asymmetric synthesis creates enantiomers selectively from the start.

concepts.title: Asymmetric Catalysis
concepts.contentHtml:
A chiral catalyst transmits its chirality to the product. A small amount of catalyst can produce a large amount of single-enantiomer product — economy embedded in the chemistry.

Sharpless asymmetric epoxidation (and dihydroxylation) — Nobel 2001. Ryoji Noyori's BINAP catalysts for asymmetric hydrogenation. William Knowles's L-DOPA synthesis (Parkinson's drug). Ben List and David MacMillan's organocatalysis (Nobel 2021).

Each is a powerful tool. Modern pharma routinely uses multiple chiral catalysts in a single synthesis route.

concepts.title: Enzymes as Chiral Catalysts
concepts.contentHtml:
Nature has been doing asymmetric catalysis with enzymes for billions of years. Enzymes deliver enantiomeric excesses near 100% — chemists envy this routinely.

Modern biocatalysis uses isolated enzymes (often engineered by directed evolution, Frances Arnold Nobel 2018) for industrial asymmetric synthesis. Sitagliptin (a diabetes drug) is now made by an evolved transaminase — replacing a rhodium-catalysed (Josiphos) asymmetric hydrogenation route.

The boundary between organic chemistry and biocatalysis blurs more each year.

title: Total Synthesis
description: Building complex natural products from scratch

concepts.title: What Is Total Synthesis?
concepts.contentHtml:
Total synthesis means building a complex natural product (typically a small molecule) from commercially available starting materials, in the lab, by chemistry alone.

It tests the limits of synthetic methodology. It also enables analog studies — once you can build the molecule, you can build variants to probe structure-activity relationships.

Famous examples: Robinson's tropinone (1917, a one-pot synthesis); Woodward's quinine (1944), strychnine (1954), chlorophyll (1960), vitamin B12 (1972). Vitamin B12 took ~100 collaborators 11 years.

concepts.title: Retrosynthesis
concepts.contentHtml:
E. J. Corey formalized the planning approach: retrosynthesis. Work backward from the target molecule, mentally disconnecting bonds and asking 'what simpler precursor could I make this from?' Repeat until you reach commercial materials.

The disconnections (called transforms) and their associated retrons are a chemist's vocabulary. Corey shared the 1990 Nobel for this systematization.

Modern AI tools (Synthia, IBM RXN, Chemical.AI) suggest retrosynthetic routes computationally, often producing creative alternatives a human might miss.

concepts.title: Modern Heroes & Limits
concepts.contentHtml:
Total synthesis remains a benchmark of synthetic chemistry. K.C. Nicolaou's syntheses (taxol, brevetoxin, calicheamicin) are encyclopedic. Phil Baran's modern syntheses emphasize step economy — getting to the target in as few operations as possible.

Some natural products are still beyond reach: complex polyketides, glycoconjugates, and biomacromolecules. Often biotechnology (engineered microbes) provides them more practically.

Total synthesis has shifted toward enabling new chemistry rather than reaching arbitrary structural targets — a benchmark sport for synthetic methodology.
